chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Business Cycle, Asset-Class Lens

lessons.title: What a Business Cycle Is and Why Asset Prices Move With It

body.text: Every rupee you invest sits inside a bigger machine: the expansion and contraction of the real economy. Learn to read that machine, and you stop being surprised by why equities, bonds, and gold keep taking turns leading.

children.text: Ask most investors what a "cycle" means and they picture a stock chart, prices swinging with sentiment. That is a market cycle. This course is about something underneath it: the business cycle, the actual expansion and contraction of production, income, and spending in the real economy. The business cycle does not show up on your broker's app, but it decides how much companies earn, what the RBI does with interest rates, and which asset class in your portfolio does the heavy lifting in any given year.
The Business Cycle Is About the Economy, Not the Ticker

markDefs.definition: Total value of goods and services produced in an economy, adjusted for inflation. The standard measure of whether an economy is actually growing.

children.text: Economists track the business cycle using real output, mainly

adjusted for inflation, along with the Index of Industrial Production (IIP), employment, and corporate order books. When GDP growth is accelerating, factories run fuller shifts, companies hire, and incomes rise. When growth slows or turns negative, the opposite happens. None of this is about whether the Nifty went up or down last week. It is about whether India actually produced and earned more this quarter than the last.

body.title: Two different clocks, often confused for one

columns.label: The business cycle (the economy)
points: Measured by GDP, IIP, employment, credit growth
Moves slowly, over quarters and years
Data arrives with a lag of weeks to months
Tells you what companies actually earned

columns.label: The market cycle (asset prices)
points: Measured by index levels, valuations, sentiment
Can move sharply in days or weeks
Prices in real time, every trading session
Tells you what investors expect companies to earn

children.text: Markets Move First. That Is the Whole Problem.

markDefs.definition: A data series or market that tends to turn before the broader economy does. Equity markets are a classic example, since prices reflect expectations rather than confirmed data.

children.text: Markets do not wait for the business cycle to show up in the data. Equity markets are a classic

, they typically start recovering months before GDP growth itself turns up, because investors are pricing in the recovery they expect, not the one that has already been confirmed. By the time IIP or GDP data confirms a slowdown is over, a large part of the market's rebound is usually already behind you. "Wait for the data to look good" is a common and expensive way to invest.
India's Growth Cycle, Year by Year
Look at India's real GDP growth over the last several years and the cycle is obvious: steady expansion, a sharp contraction, and a strong rebound, all within a few years.

body.text: The same financial year the economy contracted by roughly 6%, the Nifty delivered its best year in over a decade. That is not a contradiction, it is the leading-indicator relationship in action: markets were pricing in the reopening months before the GDP data confirmed a recovery. Notice too that FY22's outsized 9% growth looks partly spectacular because it is being compared against FY21's collapsed base. Reading one year's growth rate without checking what it is being measured against is one of the most common mistakes even experienced analysts make.

children.text: The Two Dials That Set Asset Returns: Growth and Inflation

Strip away the noise and almost every macro debate about which asset to own comes down to two dials: is growth in the economy speeding up or slowing down, and is inflation rising or falling. Every phase of the business cycle is some combination of these two dials, and each combination tends to favour a different asset class. This is often drawn as an "investment clock". We will use a simpler two-by-two grid, and build on it through every chapter of this course.

cells: Overheat: commodities and real assets usually lead

body.text: Stagflation, weak or falling growth combined with rising inflation, is the only quadrant where both equities and bonds tend to disappoint at the same time. India saw a mild version of this in 2022, when GDP growth was still positive but decelerating, while CPI inflation spiked past 7% on the back of the Russia-Ukraine war and rising crude prices.

The growth-inflation grid is a simplified teaching model, not a mechanical trading system. Real economies rarely sit in one clean quadrant, data gets revised, and the RBI's own actions shift the picture in the middle of a quarter. Use it to organise your thinking about which assets have the wind behind them, not to time entries and exits to the day.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: It's early 2021. India's GDP growth is accelerating out of the Covid contraction, and inflation is still relatively subdued. Which quadrant of the growth-inflation grid does this describe, and which asset class would the framework favour?
body.explanation: Rising growth plus falling or low inflation is the Recovery quadrant, usually the best environment for equities. This lines up with what actually happened: the Nifty had one of its strongest years on record in FY21 as the economy reopened.

body.title: The 2022 Squeeze
body.scenario: By mid-2022, Brent crude had spiked past $120 a barrel, India's CPI inflation was running above 7%, well outside the RBI's comfort zone, while GDP growth, though slowing from FY22's high base, was still positive. The RBI raised the repo rate several times through the year, from 4% to above 6%.
body.prompt: Using the growth-inflation grid, which quadrant is this closest to, and what would you expect from equities, bonds, and gold based on the framework? Then check how each one actually performed that year.
body.modelAnswer: This sits close to the overheat-to-stagflation boundary: growth was still positive but decelerating, while inflation was clearly rising. The framework would expect commodities and real assets to hold up better than financial assets, and long-duration bonds to struggle as the RBI hiked rates. In practice, the Nifty ended calendar 2022 up only modestly, around 4%, a real (inflation-adjusted) loss given CPI running above 6% for most of the year. Long-duration government bond funds saw NAVs fall as the 10-year G-sec yield rose from around 6.45% to above 7.3%. Gold in INR terms rose by low double digits, helped by rupee depreciation from about ₹74 to ₹82.7 per dollar, even though dollar gold prices were roughly flat. The framework did not predict the exact numbers, but it correctly flagged which asset class faced the biggest headwind, and which had a natural hedge built in.

children.text: The next lesson breaks the business cycle into its four classic phases, expansion, peak, contraction, and trough, with sharper markers for each. After that, we go asset class by asset class: equities and sector rotation in Chapter 2, bonds and rates in Chapter 3, gold, real estate, cash, and commodities in Chapter 4, and finally, in Chapter 5, how to put all of it into one portfolio you can actually run through a full cycle without overtrading it.

cards.definition: The recurring expansion and contraction of real economic output, measured mainly through GDP, IIP, and employment, distinct from swings in asset prices.
Total value of goods and services produced in an economy, adjusted for inflation, the standard measure of whether an economy is actually growing.
A data series or market that tends to turn before the broader economy does. Equity markets are a classic example.
A framework mapping combinations of rising or falling growth and inflation to the asset classes that tend to perform best in each combination.
A period of weak or falling growth combined with high or rising inflation, historically the hardest environment for both equities and bonds together.

body.text: GDP, IIP, and index figures in this lesson are rounded and approximate, drawn from MOSPI, RBI, and NSE data, and are provided for education only. GDP estimates are routinely revised by MOSPI after initial release. The growth-inflation framework is a simplified teaching model, not a mechanical trading system, and past patterns are no guarantee of future asset performance. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own portfolio.

points: The business cycle is about the real economy (GDP, IIP, employment), distinct from the market cycle in asset prices, though the two are closely linked
Equity markets are forward looking and typically turn before business cycle data confirms a change, which is why "waiting for good data" is often costly
India's GDP growth history shows a clear cycle: from roughly 6.5% in FY19 to a Covid contraction of about 6% in FY21 to a base-effect rebound near 9% in FY22
The Nifty rose by roughly 70% in FY21, the same year GDP contracted, a clean example of markets leading the real economy
Almost every asset-class call comes down to two dials: whether growth is rising or falling, and whether inflation is rising or falling
The growth-inflation grid gives four quadrants, recovery (equities), overheat (commodities), slowdown (bonds), and stagflation (cash), each favouring a different asset class
Stagflation is the hardest quadrant, since it tends to hurt both equities and bonds at once, which is why later chapters treat cash and gold as real portfolio tools, not afterthoughts
